Failure-aware clinical decision support

A risk model that knows when to stop. Three small agents decide whether the AI may answer a case on its own or must pass it to a clinician.

Team repository on GitHub

The problem

A risk model hands back a probability for every patient, including the ones it should not be answering. In a clinic the costly errors are confident wrong ones, and a plain classifier cannot tell you which cases those are.

This project asks a narrower question than "how accurate is it". Given a model that predicts in-hospital death at admission, can a thin safety layer spot the cases that need a person and send them over? The agents here are plain rules, with no language model involved.

This is a team project for CS 5130. My CV lists the three-agent pipeline and the PCA out-of-distribution check as my part of it. The repo's commit history is under my teammate's account, so I only describe what the code does.

How it works

  1. Predict.A logistic regression on admission-time facts (admission type, insurance, language, age and similar) gives the probability of in-hospital death.
  2. Propose.The Proposer labels it high risk at 0.7 or above, low at 0.3 or below, else intermediate.
  3. Doubt.The Skeptic raises a flag if the probability is within 0.4 to 0.6, if the binary entropy is above 0.90 bits, or if the case sits beyond the 95th percentile of PCA distance from the training data.
  4. Decide.A flag means hand off. Without one, the harness alerts at 0.85 or above, clears at 0.15 or below and hands off everything in between.

Results

Results from one run on MIMIC-IV
MeasureValue
AUROC0.871
Brier score0.019
Mortality prevalenceabout 2.2%
Handed to a clinicianabout 7.1%
AI decided aloneabout 92.9%
True deaths escalatedabout 29.7%
False negatives escalatedabout 28.5%

Source: the repository README, which reports these from one run on a 70/30 stratified split. The cohort is MIMIC-IV v3.1, 546K hospitalizations (my CV).

Limits and next steps

  • Mortality is rare (about 2.2%). A model that gave everyone the base rate would score a Brier of roughly 0.0215 (0.022 x 0.978), so 0.019 is a small gain over knowing nothing. AUROC is the better evidence here.
  • Roughly 7 in 10 true deaths are still decided by the AI alone, and the same holds for the false negatives. The harness catches a meaningful share of dangerous errors. It does not catch most.
  • The features are demographics and admission facts only, with post-outcome fields removed to avoid leakage. It is a study of failure-aware behavior, not a deployable predictor.
  • Figures come from one run with no confidence intervals. Thresholds were set by hand and not tuned against a cost model.
  • The repo also holds a ResNet-50 retinal classifier on BRSET (average AUROC about 0.76), which is a separate pipeline.
